definition: The simulation of human intelligence processes by computer systems, including learning, reasoning, and self-correction.
A subset of AI where systems learn from data to improve performance on a task without being explicitly programmed for it.
A subfield of machine learning using neural networks with many layers (deep networks) to learn hierarchical representations from raw data.
A neural network trained on vast text corpora to understand and generate human language. Examples include GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and LLaMA.
A class of LLM developed by OpenAI that uses the Transformer architecture, pre-trained on large text corpora and fine-tuned for various tasks.
A neural network architecture introduced in 'Attention is All You Need' (2017) that uses self-attention mechanisms instead of recurrence. Foundation of most modern LLMs.
A technique allowing a model to weigh the relevance of different parts of the input when producing each part of the output. Core component of the Transformer.
An architecture that combines a retrieval system (searching a knowledge base) with a generative LLM to produce grounded, up-to-date responses.
A computational model loosely inspired by biological neurons, composed of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons) that learn weight adjustments through training.
A deep learning architecture that applies learned convolutional filters to detect local patterns. Dominant in image classification and computer vision.
A neural network with loops that allow information to persist across time steps. Used for sequential data like text and time series.
A type of RNN that uses gating mechanisms to selectively remember or forget information over long sequences, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem.
A framework where a generator network and a discriminator network compete: the generator tries to produce realistic data; the discriminator tries to detect fakes.
A generative model that encodes inputs into a latent probability distribution and decodes samples from it, enabling smooth generation of new data.
A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process to generate high-quality images or other data. Basis of Stable Diffusion and DALL·E 2.
A training technique where human preference rankings are used to fine-tune a language model via a reward model, aligning model outputs with human values.
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a labelled dataset of (prompt, ideal response) pairs. Typically the first stage before RLHF alignment.
A policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm used in RLHF to update the LLM policy without taking excessively large update steps.
An alignment technique that fine-tunes LLMs directly on human preference pairs without a separate reward model, simpler than RLHF+PPO.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that injects small trainable rank-decomposition matrices into frozen model weights, drastically reducing training cost.
A variant of LoRA that fine-tunes a quantized (4-bit) base model, enabling LLM fine-tuning on consumer GPUs.
The practice of crafting input prompts to elicit desired outputs from an LLM without modifying model weights.
A prompting strategy where a small number of labelled examples are included in the prompt to guide the model toward the desired format or task.
Using an LLM for a task without any examples in the prompt, relying solely on the model's pre-trained knowledge.
A prompting technique where the model is instructed to show step-by-step reasoning before giving a final answer, improving accuracy on complex tasks.
The basic unit of text processed by an LLM. A token is roughly 3–4 characters or 0.75 words in English. Context length is measured in tokens.
The maximum number of tokens an LLM can process in a single forward pass (input + output combined). Limits how much text the model can 'see' at once.
A dense numerical vector representation of text (or other data) in a high-dimensional space where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity.
A database optimised for storing and querying high-dimensional embedding vectors using approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search. Core component of RAG systems.
When an LLM generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or fabricated information. A key challenge in production LLM deployments.
A sampling parameter that controls the randomness of an LLM's output. Higher values produce more varied responses; lower values produce more deterministic ones.
A decoding strategy where the model samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. Balances diversity and coherence.
The process of continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialise its behaviour.
A technique where a model trained on one task is reused as the starting point for a model on a different but related task.
The initial large-scale training phase where a model learns general representations from a massive dataset before any task-specific fine-tuning.
A component that splits raw text into tokens and maps them to integer IDs for input to an LLM. Vocabulary size and tokenization strategy affect model behaviour.
The fixed set of tokens a model knows. Tokens outside the vocabulary are split into sub-word units by the tokenizer (e.g. BPE, WordPiece).
A subword tokenization algorithm that iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent byte pairs. Used by GPT and many other LLMs.
A metric measuring how well a language model predicts a sample of text. Lower perplexity indicates better predictive performance.
An automatic metric for evaluating machine-generated text (especially translation) by comparing n-gram overlaps with human reference texts.
A set of metrics for evaluating automatic summarisation by measuring n-gram and longest common subsequence overlaps with reference summaries.
A standardised test or dataset used to evaluate and compare model performance on a defined task (e.g. MMLU, HellaSwag, HumanEval).
A benchmark testing LLM knowledge across 57 academic subjects including STEM, humanities, and social sciences.
A benchmark of 164 Python programming problems used to evaluate LLMs' code generation ability.
When a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, and fails to generalise to unseen data. Detected by a gap between training and validation loss.
When a model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data, resulting in poor performance on both training and validation sets.
Techniques (e.g. L1/L2, dropout) applied during training to reduce overfitting by penalising model complexity or randomly disabling neurons.
A regularisation technique that randomly sets a fraction of neuron activations to zero during training, preventing co-adaptation and reducing overfitting.
A technique that normalises layer inputs within a mini-batch during training, stabilising and accelerating deep network training.
A hyperparameter controlling the step size of gradient descent weight updates. Too high causes divergence; too low causes slow convergence.
An optimisation algorithm that iteratively adjusts model parameters in the direction of the negative gradient of the loss function.
A widely used gradient descent optimiser that adapts learning rates per parameter using estimates of first and second moments of the gradients.
A function measuring the discrepancy between model predictions and ground truth labels. Minimised during training. Examples: cross-entropy, MSE.
A loss function commonly used for classification tasks that measures the difference between predicted probability distributions and true labels.
An activation function applied to the final layer of a classifier that converts raw logits into a probability distribution over classes.
An activation function defined as max(0, x). Widely used in deep networks for its simplicity and effectiveness in mitigating the vanishing gradient problem.
An activation function that maps any real number to (0, 1). Used in binary classification output layers and historically in hidden layers.
A parameter set before training begins (e.g. learning rate, batch size, number of layers) as opposed to model weights learned during training.
One complete pass through the entire training dataset during training.
The number of training examples used in one forward/backward pass before updating model weights.
A processor with thousands of small cores optimised for the parallel matrix operations that dominate deep learning training and inference.
Google's custom ASIC designed specifically for large-scale neural network training and inference, offering high throughput for matrix multiplications.
The process of running a trained model on new inputs to produce predictions. Distinct from training, typically much faster and cheaper.
Reducing the numerical precision of model weights (e.g. from float32 to int8 or int4) to decrease memory usage and increase inference speed, with minimal accuracy loss.
Removing redundant or low-importance weights from a trained neural network to reduce model size and inference cost.
Training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the outputs of a larger 'teacher' model, transferring knowledge into a more efficient form.
An open format for representing machine learning models, enabling interoperability between frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow.
An LLM-based system that can perceive inputs, plan actions, use tools (e.g. web search, code execution), and iterate to complete multi-step tasks autonomously.
The capability of an LLM to call external functions or APIs (e.g. calculators, databases, web search) to augment its reasoning with real-world information.
An open protocol by Anthropic standardising how LLM applications connect to external tools, data sources, and context providers.
The iterative cycle in an AI agent where the model reasons, selects a tool action, receives the result, and reasons again until the task is complete.
Describes AI models that process and generate multiple data types — typically text, images, audio, or video — within a single model.
A model trained specifically to produce dense vector representations of text (or other data) for use in semantic search, clustering, and RAG pipelines.
Search that retrieves results based on the meaning of a query rather than exact keyword matches, typically using embedding similarity.
A family of algorithms (e.g. HNSW, IVF) that find vectors close to a query vector in high-dimensional space faster than exhaustive search, used in vector databases.
A language model with far fewer parameters than frontier LLMs (typically <10B), designed to run efficiently on-device or at lower cost.
A category of fine-tuning techniques (including LoRA, prefix tuning, adapters) that update only a small fraction of model parameters, reducing compute and memory.
An attack where malicious text in the model's input overrides the system prompt or intended instructions, causing unintended model behaviour.
A prompting technique designed to bypass an LLM's safety guidelines and elicit responses the model was trained to refuse.
The field of research and engineering focused on ensuring AI systems pursue goals and exhibit behaviours intended by their designers and beneficial to humanity.
Mechanisms — input/output filters, classifiers, constitutional rules — applied around an LLM to prevent harmful, off-topic, or policy-violating outputs.
Instructions provided to an LLM at the start of a conversation (often hidden from the end user) that set the model's persona, rules, and context.
Hypothetical AI capable of performing a broad range of intellectual tasks at or beyond human capability; no universally accepted test establishes AGI.
AI designed for a limited set of tasks or a specific domain rather than general-purpose intelligence.
Hypothetical AI whose general intellectual capabilities substantially exceed those of humans across most domains.
AI systems that generate new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code.
A broadly trained model that can be adapted to many downstream tasks through prompting, fine-tuning, or additional training.
The field of AI concerned with processing, understanding, and generating human language.
Language technology focused on interpreting meaning, intent, entities, and relationships in text or speech.
Generating human-readable language from structured data, representations, or model outputs.
Identifying and classifying entities such as people, organizations, locations, and dates in text.
Converting spoken audio into written text.
Generating spoken audio from written text.
Detecting and converting text in images or scanned documents into machine-readable text.
A model trained to process or relate visual inputs and language, supporting tasks such as image question answering.
An LLM extended to process multiple modalities such as text and images, and sometimes audio or video.
A Transformer-based language model pretrained using bidirectional context and adapted for language understanding tasks.
A model framework that treats many NLP tasks as text-to-text problems.
A denoising sequence-to-sequence model trained to reconstruct corrupted text.
A BERT-style model trained with modified data, optimization, and masking choices.
A family of large language models released by Meta; available terms and permitted uses depend on each model's license.
A model training approach that aligns image and text representations using contrastive learning.
A vision architecture that divides images into patches and processes their representations with Transformer layers.
A family of object-detection models that predict object locations and classes in a single network evaluation.
A family of image segmentation models designed to produce masks from prompts such as points or boxes.
A metric that averages precision-recall performance across classes and sometimes detection thresholds.
The overlap between two regions divided by their union; used in detection and segmentation evaluation.
A speech transcription metric based on substitutions, deletions, and insertions divided by reference word count.
A text recognition metric based on character substitutions, deletions, and insertions relative to a reference.
The average squared difference between predicted values and target values, commonly used for regression.
The average absolute difference between predicted values and target values.
The square root of mean squared error, expressed in the target variable's units.
A metric often referring to area under a ROC curve, summarizing ranking performance across thresholds.
A curve plotting true-positive rate against false-positive rate across classification thresholds.
A curve showing the trade-off between precision and recall across classification thresholds.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when both false positives and false negatives matter.
The proportion of positive results that are true positives; it depends on sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence.
The proportion of negative results that are true negatives; it depends on sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence.
An input that differs materially from the distribution represented in a model's training or validation data.
A dimensionality-reduction method that projects data onto orthogonal directions capturing maximal variance.
A nonlinear dimensionality-reduction method often used to visualize high-dimensional data.
A nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique that emphasizes local neighborhood structure for visualization.

full_form: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise
definition: A density-based clustering algorithm that groups closely packed points and identifies low-density points as noise.
A gradient-boosted tree library designed for efficient, regularized predictive modeling.
A gradient-boosting framework designed for efficient tree learning, including histogram-based methods.
A gradient-boosting library with techniques designed to handle categorical features.
A method that creates synthetic minority-class examples by interpolating between selected minority examples.
A graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor indexing algorithm for efficient vector similarity search.
A lexical ranking function based on query-term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document-length normalization.
A ranking metric that rewards relevant results near the top of a list and normalizes against an ideal ranking.
A ranking metric averaging the reciprocal rank of the first relevant result across queries.
An evaluation framework for RAG systems with metrics for faithfulness, answer relevance, and context quality.
A retrieval approach that uses graph relationships or graph-derived summaries to organize context for generation.
A retrieval approach combining lexical search with semantic vector search.
A model or algorithm that re-scores an initial result set to improve relevance ordering.
A model that jointly processes a query and candidate document to produce a relevance score.
A model that independently encodes queries and documents into vectors for efficient retrieval.
Splitting source documents into smaller passages for indexing or model context while balancing coherence and retrieval precision.
Connecting model responses to trusted data, evidence, or tool results so claims are better supported.
The degree to which a generated answer is supported by supplied context rather than unsupported claims.
A measure of how directly an answer addresses a question, distinct from factual correctness.
An agent pattern that interleaves reasoning-oriented steps with actions and observations from tools or an environment.
A protocol for communication and collaboration between AI agents.
A machine-readable specification for describing HTTP APIs and supporting documentation and client generation.
A vocabulary for describing and validating the structure and constraints of JSON data.
Model output constrained or validated to follow a defined structure, such as a JSON schema.
A generation technique that restricts possible token sequences to satisfy a grammar, schema, or formal constraint.
Practices and tooling for developing, deploying, evaluating, monitoring, and governing LLM applications.
A managed catalog of model versions and associated metadata, metrics, lineage, and deployment status.
Documentation describing a model's intended uses, evaluation, limitations, and risks.
A change over time in the statistical properties of input data that can reduce model reliability.
A change over time in the relationship between inputs and target outcomes.
A system for managing, sharing, serving, and tracking features used by ML training and inference pipelines.
Unintended use of information during training that would not legitimately be available at prediction time, inflating evaluation results.
Methods that discourage overly complex models or parameter values to improve generalization.
A technique that normalizes intermediate activations using batch statistics during training.
A technique that normalizes activations across features within an example, widely used in Transformers.
A smooth activation function used in many Transformer models.
An optimization algorithm that estimates gradients from examples or mini-batches to update model parameters.
An optimizer that maintains moving averages of gradients and squared gradients to adapt parameter update sizes.
A technique that limits gradient magnitude to reduce unstable or excessively large parameter updates.
An algorithm that computes gradients of a neural network loss with respect to its parameters using the chain rule.
Summing gradients over multiple smaller batches before updating parameters to simulate a larger effective batch.
A distributed training strategy that replicates a model across devices, splits batches, and combines gradients or updates.
A strategy that splits model tensors or operations across multiple devices.
A strategy that partitions model layers across devices and schedules microbatches through stages.
A distributed training approach that shards model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers.
Memory optimization techniques that shard optimizer states and sometimes gradients and parameters across workers.
A 16-bit floating-point format used to reduce memory and accelerate neural-network computation.
A 16-bit floating-point format with a wider exponent range than FP16, commonly used in deep learning.
A 32-bit floating-point representation used for model parameters and numerically sensitive operations.
An 8-bit integer representation used in quantized weights or activations, with accuracy and hardware trade-offs.
A model file format used by llama.cpp and related tools to package model weights and metadata.
An LLM serving engine designed for efficient inference, including memory-efficient attention and continuous batching.
A toolkit for deploying and serving text-generation models through production-oriented inference endpoints.
A tool for downloading, running, and managing language models locally through a developer-friendly interface.
A platform for managing ML experiments, packaging models, tracking artifacts, and supporting model lifecycle workflows.
A toolkit for building and operating machine-learning workflows on Kubernetes.
A platform for serving ML models on Kubernetes with standardized inference interfaces and scaling features.
A framework for packaging and deploying machine-learning models as production services.
A distributed computing framework for scaling Python applications, including ML training, tuning, and serving.
A graph with directed edges and no directed cycles, often used to represent pipeline dependencies.
A data integration pattern that extracts data, transforms it, and loads it into a destination.
A data integration pattern that loads raw data into a target platform before transforming it there.
A column-oriented file format designed for efficient storage and retrieval of structured data.
A data architecture combining aspects of data lakes and warehouses, aiming to support flexible storage with reliable table semantics.
Artificially generated data intended to reproduce selected properties of real data for testing, development, or analysis.
A strategy that selects informative unlabeled examples for annotation to reduce labeling effort.
A learning approach that creates supervision signals from the data itself, such as predicting hidden or transformed inputs.
A training approach in which participants train locally and share model updates rather than centralizing raw data.
A formal privacy framework that bounds how much an analysis output can depend on any one individual's data.
Individually identifiable health information protected under applicable HIPAA rules when handled by covered entities or business associates.
Software intended for one or more medical purposes that performs those purposes without being part of a hardware medical device, subject to applicable definitions.
Principles for developing, validating, deploying, and monitoring ML-enabled medical-device software throughout its lifecycle.
Evaluation of a model on data from a separate institution, period, or setting to assess generalization beyond development data.
Evaluation using data collected forward in time or during a planned study after the protocol is defined.
The extent to which use of a model or intervention improves meaningful decisions or outcomes in its intended setting.
Practices and tooling for deploying, monitoring, governing, and maintaining ML systems throughout their lifecycle.
A formal agreement defining service commitments such as availability, support response, and remedies.
A measurable target for a service-level indicator over a specified time window.
A quantitative measure of service behavior, such as request success rate, latency, or freshness.
Time from sending a prompt to receiving the first generated token, an important interactive latency metric.
A throughput measure describing how many tokens a model generates per second.
A cache of attention keys and values from previous tokens that reduces repeated computation during autoregressive generation.
An inference optimization where a smaller draft model proposes tokens that a larger model verifies.
A serving technique that dynamically adds and removes sequences from batches as requests arrive or finish.
Elapsed time between a request or input and its response or output.
Amount of work completed per unit time, such as requests or tokens processed per second.
Selecting among available models based on task, quality, latency, availability, or cost.
A cache that reuses responses for queries considered semantically similar, subject to relevance thresholds and correctness safeguards.
A resilience pattern that temporarily blocks calls to a failing dependency to prevent cascading failures.
An identifier used by a server to recognize retries of the same operation and avoid duplicate side effects.
A control that caps requests or usage by a user, client, or organization over a defined interval.
Controls that prevent one customer's users or processes from accessing another customer's data or resources.
An authorization model that grants permissions based on roles assigned to users or groups.
An authorization model that evaluates user, resource, action, and context attributes against policies.
An identity layer built on OAuth 2.0 that lets clients verify end-user identity and obtain standardized claims.
A framework enabling an application to obtain limited access to an HTTP service on behalf of a user or itself.
A compact token format for representing claims, often signed or encrypted, used in authentication and authorization.
A database feature that restricts which rows a database role or session can read or modify according to policies.
A standard protocol for automating user and group provisioning between identity providers and applications.
An XML-based standard commonly used to exchange authentication and authorization data between identity and service providers.
An authentication arrangement that lets users access multiple applications through a shared identity provider session.
Authentication requiring two or more distinct factor types, such as knowledge, possession, or inherence.
A browser mechanism controlling whether a webpage may read cross-origin responses; it does not replace server-side authorization.
An attack that tricks a browser into sending an unwanted authenticated request to a site where the user is signed in.
A vulnerability class in which attacker-controlled content executes as script in another user's browser context.
A cryptographic protocol that protects data in transit and authenticates servers, and optionally clients.
A security control that inspects HTTP traffic and applies rules to detect or block certain web attacks and abusive requests.
A machine-readable inventory of software components and dependencies included in a product or build.
Security analysis of source code or compiled code without executing the application.
Security testing performed against a running application to identify vulnerabilities observable during execution.
A threat-modeling framework covering spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege.
A public identifier system for publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
A standardized framework for communicating the severity characteristics of software vulnerabilities.
A family of explanation methods that use Shapley values to attribute a prediction to input features.
A method that approximates a model locally with an interpretable surrogate to explain an individual prediction.
A NIST framework to help organizations identify, assess, and manage risks associated with AI systems.
An EU regulation establishing a risk-based legal framework for AI systems, with obligations depending on system type and use.
A design in which a person reviews, approves, corrects, or directs selected steps in an automated workflow.
Structured adversarial testing intended to discover safety, security, reliability, or misuse weaknesses.
Prompt injection carried by untrusted external content such as retrieved documents, webpages, or emails.
An attack that attempts to infer sensitive properties or reconstruct training information from model outputs or access.
An attack that attempts to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data.
A description for models whose trained weights are downloadable; this does not necessarily mean training data or code are open.
Information about where data originated, how it was collected or transformed, and how it moved through a pipeline.
Recording parameters, code versions, datasets, metrics, artifacts, and outcomes for training or evaluation runs.
A saved snapshot of model parameters and training state that can be restored for continued training or evaluation.
Stopping training when a monitored validation metric stops improving, often to reduce overfitting or wasted compute.
Tracking prompt changes so teams can compare behavior, reproduce results, and roll back problematic revisions.
A record of steps in an AI request, such as model calls, tool invocations, retrieval, timing, and errors.
A timed unit of work within a trace, such as a model call, retrieval query, or tool invocation.
An open standard and toolkit for generating, collecting, and exporting traces, metrics, and logs.
Estimated model and infrastructure cost attributable to a single request based on usage and pricing.
A configured limit on input and output token consumption for a request, workflow, or billing period.
A repeatable framework that runs test cases against a model or application and collects results and metrics.
A curated collection of representative test examples with expected outcomes or reviewer guidance for regression evaluation.
Overlap between benchmark content and training or tuning data that can inflate measured performance.
An approach that prioritizes systematic improvements to data quality, coverage, and labeling to improve AI performance.
Creating, transforming, or selecting input variables to help a model learn useful signal.
The reference value, annotation, or outcome treated as correct for training or evaluating a model.
A measure of consistency among people labeling the same data, using a statistic appropriate to the task.
A statistic measuring agreement between two annotators while accounting for agreement expected by chance under its assumptions.
A process for resolving disagreements between annotators or reviewers to produce a consistent reference label.
A condition in which classes occur at substantially different frequencies, which can affect training and evaluation.
A decision boundary applied to a model score or probability to assign a predicted class or action.
A framework that uses calibration data to construct prediction sets or intervals with stated coverage guarantees under assumptions.
Uncertainty associated with limited knowledge or model parameters, which may decrease with more informative data.
Uncertainty arising from inherent noise or variability in the data-generating process.
An architecture with multiple expert networks and a routing mechanism that selects which experts process each input.
A positional encoding technique applying position-dependent rotations to query and key representations in attention.
An exact attention algorithm designed to reduce memory traffic and improve attention computation efficiency.
An attention variant that shares key-value heads across groups of query heads to reduce cache memory and inference bandwidth.
An attention variant where multiple query heads share a single key and value head.
An attention mechanism that computes multiple attention representations in parallel and combines their outputs.
A tokenizer/detokenizer library that can train subword models directly from raw text.
A model capability or configuration supporting a large number of tokens in a request, subject to model-specific limits.
Methods that reduce conversation or retrieved content while attempting to preserve information relevant to the task.
Mechanisms that store or retrieve information across steps or sessions so an agent can use relevant prior context.
Selecting and ordering actions to reach a goal, sometimes with plans revised using feedback.
An agent pattern that creates a plan and executes steps, potentially revising the plan based on intermediate results.
A system in which multiple agents interact or coordinate to solve tasks, potentially with specialized roles.
A workflow execution model that persists progress and can recover from restarts without losing completed work.
An AI workflow in which a model interacts with a graphical interface through permitted actions such as clicking and typing.
An isolated environment that limits permissions and resources available to untrusted or potentially unsafe code.
A principle granting each user, process, or component only the permissions needed for its intended tasks.
Unauthorized transfer of data from a system, potentially through outputs, tools, network calls, or compromised workflows.
An input deliberately or unintentionally modified to cause a model to make an incorrect or unexpected prediction.
Unintended disclosure of system instructions, templates, or other prompt content through model responses or application behavior.
Legal terms governing permitted use, modification, redistribution, or commercial deployment of model weights and related materials.
An API endpoint that accepts inputs and returns predictions or generated outputs from a deployed model.
Running predictions over a collection of inputs in an asynchronous or scheduled job rather than responding to each request interactively.
Serving predictions in response to live requests, typically with latency requirements.
Running AI computation on or near the device or location where data is generated.
AI processing performed directly on a user's device rather than requiring a remote model service for every operation.
Delay incurred when a service or model initializes, loads weights, or allocates resources before processing a request.
A mechanism that slows upstream producers when downstream components cannot process work at the incoming rate.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured as a time interval after a disruptive event.
The target maximum duration for restoring a service after a disruption.
Collecting and processing only the data needed for a defined purpose to reduce privacy and security exposure.
Removing or transforming identifiers to reduce the likelihood that data can be linked to an individual; some re-identification risk may remain.
Processing intended to make data no longer identifiable by reasonably likely means under the applicable legal standard.
Requirements or commitments about the geographic location where data is stored or processed.
A time-ordered record of relevant actions and changes supporting investigation, accountability, and governance.
Measures that let people monitor, intervene in, or override an AI system when appropriate to its risk and use case.
An assessment of potential effects of an AI system on people, groups, organizations, or society using a defined framework.

Embedding an AI system into clinical or operational processes, including interfaces, escalation paths, and responsibility for actions.

A controlled change to model weights, code, configuration, prompts, or dependencies that may affect system behavior.

A browser security mechanism restricting permitted sources and behaviors for scripts, styles, and other resources.
A policy instructing browsers to use HTTPS for a site for a specified period.
Verifying a token's signature and required claims, such as issuer and expiration, before trusting it.
A session practice in which a refresh token is replaced during refresh, with reuse detection helping identify possible theft.
A service for storing, controlling access to, auditing, and rotating credentials and API keys.
A service for creating, storing, controlling, and auditing cryptographic keys.
Encryption applied to stored data such as disks, databases, or backups.
Protection of data while moving across networks, typically using TLS.

Values that are unavailable or unrecorded; the missingness mechanism affects appropriate analysis methods.
